title: Cambodia's killing years
hookLine: the Khmer Rouge closed the monasteries and killed monks; the sangha was rebuilt from very few

cards: A monk can't ordain himself. In the Theravada tradition, a new monk is received by a gathering of monks already ordained, chanting together, so the robe passes hand to hand in an unbroken line.

Usually that line is so ordinary nobody thinks about it. Then comes a time when the gathering itself almost disappears. What happens to a tradition when there are hardly enough monks left to make a new one?

teach.b: In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge took power and set out to remake the whole country from nothing. Cities were emptied. Money, schools and markets were abolished.
Religion was treated as an enemy. Monasteries were closed or turned into prisons and storehouses. Monks were forced out of their robes, sent to labor in the fields, and killed.
Old palm-leaf texts were burned or left to rot. It is hard to say how much was lost.

teach.h: REBUILT FROM THE FEW WHO WERE LEFT.
teach.b: When the regime fell, the sangha, the community of monks, had to be rebuilt from the few who were left: monks who had survived by hiding, or in exile, or by putting the robe aside. Ordinations began again.
Monasteries reopened, sometimes in buildings that still bore the marks of what had been done there.
One monk who survived abroad, Maha Ghosananda, came home and led peace walks across the country, monks, nuns and lay people side by side through places still scarred by war.
He taught that peace is made the way a walk is made, step by step, and each step can be a meditation. After those years, that was not a pleasant gesture. It was a hard choice about what to rebuild.
And it shows this: a line of practice can come close to breaking and still continue.
The gathering grew again, one ordination at a time, until there were monks enough to receive the next.

how: Cambodian Buddhists remember those years at ceremonies for the dead and at the monasteries that were rebuilt, and monks and lay people have kept up walks and gatherings for peace.

practice: Bring to mind a community that was broken and came back, Cambodia's monasteries, a congregation after a fire, a neighborhood after a flood, a family after a hard year, and picture the first few people who showed up again, before anyone knew it would work.
With each in-breath, notice their courage; with each out-breath, offer them thanks. If grief comes for what was lost, let it be there; it belongs in this too.

wordCard.voice: Upasampada. The full ordination that nearly disappeared when Cambodia's sangha was almost destroyed, and that the few who were left began to give again. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali upasampadā: full ordination, given by a gathering of monks; in Cambodia it began again from few.

carryVoice: Your line: rebuilt from few. A line close to breaking, still unbroken. See you tomorrow.
